Deployment practice · settlement path

Rehearse the rollback

A rollback plan nobody has run is a hypothesis. Forty-five minutes a month turns it into a runbook with a known duration — and forces the schema decisions that make rolling back safe in the first place.

The problem is the schema, not the deploy

Redeploying the previous image is a CI job. It takes two minutes and it does not require judgment. The part that decides whether a bad release becomes an incident or a bad afternoon is a different question: what did the version you are rolling back write while it was up, and can the previous release read it?

On the settlement path at Harborline Freight, the last rollback before we started drilling took two hours forty minutes and cost about six minutes of settlement events, which became a reconciliation project. Fourteen months and eleven drills later, the next real rollback on that path took eleven minutes and lost nothing.

That is a before and an after, and it is one data point. What follows is the mechanism, the drill, and what the drill costs — because the mechanism is the part that generalizes and the eleven minutes is not.

The mechanism: expand-contract, never a down-migration

Every schema change ships in two releases, and the old path stays readable the whole time.

  1. Expand. Add the new column. Dual-write to both. Backfill. The previous release still reads and writes the old path and does not know anything happened.
  2. Switch. Release two moves reads to the new column. Writes stay dual.
  3. Contract. Drop the old column in a third release — or never. Several of ours are still dual-writing because the deletion was not worth the risk.

The property this buys: at any moment the previous release can read the current schema. Rolling back is therefore redeploying an image plus flipping a feature flag off, and both are states the system has already run. No down-migrations, no schema surgery at 2am, no "restore from snapshot and lose the last hour."

Feature flags default off and are flipped after the deploy is healthy. The flag state lives in the config service while the image lives in the deploy pipeline, which is why a rollback is two steps and not one: the two systems can disagree, and the runbook names which one is authoritative.

The part that breaks: backfills

Dual-writes are safe. Backfilling forty million rows is not instant, and rolling back mid-backfill leaves a column that is partially populated — harmless to the old code, which ignores it, and harmful to the new code when it comes back. So backfills are batched by key range with a checkpoint row, and the batch is resumable.

We know this because a drill found it. That is the argument for the drill in one sentence.

The drill

Forty-five minutes, first Tuesday of the month, same runbook, same path, staging with production-shaped data. Three roles: two run it, one watches the clock and the error rate. The person running it rotates monthly, and somebody who ran it last month does not run it this month. The rotation is the point — if the same person always runs the drill you are rehearsing that person, not the team.

The runbook is numbered, with an owner per step and an explicit decision point:

  1. Call it. One named person says go, and says what triggered it.
  2. Flip the feature flag off. Confirm in the config service, not in the app logs.
  3. Redeploy the previous image. Watch the error rate for three minutes.
  4. Answer the data question out loud: what did the rolled-back version write, and can the current schema be read by the code now running?
  5. Close it with a duration and at least one finding.

Every drill has to find something. Not something large. If a drill finds nothing, the runbook is wrong, because a runbook that never surprises anyone is a runbook nobody is reading. The log for the last four months includes: the flag service timing out at 400ms when we had budgeted 50; a backfill checkpoint row that was not resumable; and a decision point where both people running the drill looked at the same dashboard and read it differently.

What it costs

CostAmountNote
Drill time45 min × 3 people, monthly~27 person-hours a year per path
Expand-contract taxone extra release per schema changethe real cost; paid whether or not you drill
Staging dataproduction-shaped, refreshed monthlya drill against toy data rehearses nothing
Social costtwo months of "this is theater"one engineer said so in a retro, out loud; we kept it and added the must-find-something rule

We ruled out automatic rollback on an error-budget breach, which is the obvious thing to build and which several tools will sell you. On this path the decision is never only "is the error rate up." It is "did we write money down in a way the previous version can read," and that needs a human. A human who has run the drill takes about four minutes to make the call. A human who has not takes twenty and asks someone else.

Where this does not generalize

We picked the path we were most afraid of and gave it a runbook, a rotation, and staging data shaped like production. Those are resources most services do not get. The honest claim is therefore narrow: a rehearsed rollback on a backward-compatible schema is fast, and the rehearsal is affordable on a path someone cares about.

The open question is what the cheap version looks like for the other twelve services. We do not have an answer yet. The current guess is a quarterly drill and a shared runbook template, which is untested and should be read as a guess.

Verdict

Run the drill monthly on one path, rotate the operator, require a finding, and pay the expand-contract tax that makes it safe. Stop when the schema stops changing — which on a settlement path is never — or when six consecutive drills find nothing, which means the runbook has gone stale and needs rewriting.
